The goal of this work is to evaluate cognitive-level semantics, such as intent and sentiment. The authors collect open-source datasets (e.g. videos, audios, etc) that have already been annotated along a particular dimension and evaluate VLMs on those tasks. In their evaluation, they use three methods: (1) zero-shot prompting, (2) SFT (where they train a model on each task separately), and (3) instruction-tuning, where they fine-tune on a mixture of tasks. The best models don’t reach 60% accuracy, which highlights why this is an important area to benchmark VLMs.

Overall, reviewers have an anonymous agreement in favor of accepting the paper. The authors confirm that all source datasets provide a permissive license for research. I encourage the authors to include their detailed breakdown of demographic representation in the dataset (mentioned in the rebuttal), such as by gender. Also, as highlighted by some reviewers, it would be good to elaborate more in the revised version on the: (1) motivation behind evaluating cognitive-level semantics, and (2) the choice of the 6 dimensions.

author_final_remarks.value:
**Summary of Our Contributions**

1. We propose MMLA, **the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating the cognitive-level capabilities of foundation models in multimodal language analysis**. It assesses six semantic dimensions across nine publicly available representative multimodal datasets, comprising 76 hours of videos.

2. We conduct comprehensive experiments with nine mainstream open-source MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2-VL), LLMs (e.g., LLaMA-3), and a closed-source MLLM (GPT-4o), using three evaluation strategies: Zero-shot Inference, Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT), and Instruction Tuning (IT).

3. This benchmark reveals a series of new insights (e.g., small MLLMs can rival large ones after SFT; comparable performance of MLLMs between SFT and IT), demonstrating the great potential of lightweight MLLMs for generalization in cognitive-level multi-tasks while greatly reducing resource costs. Moreover, the performance of all models still averages below 70%, indicating both the significance and the challenge of this benchmark.

MMLA establishes an original and solid basis for evaluating foundation models in multimodal language analysis, **pushing the limits and guiding the development directions of existing MLLMs**.

**Summary of Reviewer Comments and Our Rebuttals**

The **original ratings are 5 (V8FD), 4 (2Cfx), 4 (QJvB), and 2 (Rbbb)**. After our detailed rebuttals, **reviewers Rbbb and 2Cfx increase their ratings**. We find reviewer Rbbb’s negative evaluation is likely due to misunderstandings regarding the motivations and contributions of our paper. After we clarify these points with supporting evidence, **Rbbb acknowledge our efforts and state all concerns have been addressed**. Besides, we conduct experiments with different random seeds to demonstrate the reliability of our results, and provide more details on the datasets and open-source release. **Reviewer 2Cfx recognize these efforts and comment that the rebuttal greatly strengthened the paper**. Reviewer QJvB’s comments are similar to 2Cfx’s, and we address all of these concerns, although there are no follow-up comments.

We also address all the conerns of the ethics review: (1) We ensure fully restricted use of all open-source datasets without further modification, (2) legal and fair use of short videos for research purposes, (3) full respect for original copyrights in redistribution, and (4) inclusion of diverse human races, ages, and genders, with detailed statistics.

**Summary of the reply to Ethics Review**: 

Across most datasets, there is a gender balance, and the datasets include individuals of various racial and ethnic backgrounds (e.g., Indian, African American, White, Asian, Caucasian, Hispanic). The age range spans approximately 24–70 years. Therefore, we believe the datasets are demographically representative and not biased, making them suitable for generalization to real-world applications.

Finally, we would like to emphasize that **the purpose of this benchmark is to explore the capabilities of foundation models in understanding human-level semantics**. The selected datasets are well-established in subfields of multimodal language analysis (e.g., emotion recognition, sentiment analysis, intent classification, humor and sarcasm detection). **The original dataset authors have taken measures to protect privacy, including consulting legal experts to ensure that short video clips fall under fair use**.

Additionally, all datasets are distributed under various licenses. **Our benchmark adheres to the strictest among them (i.e., CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) for research purposes only. We do not modify or redistribute any original materials**. All redistribution is in accordance with license terms.

We have provided the most complete demographic statistics available for each dataset. These statistics support that the benchmark does not exhibit race, gender, age, or other forms of bias. This information will be included in the final version of the paper.

We believe our use of publicly available datasets is fully permitted, legal, and in accordance with standard academic practice. We hope this response addresses your concerns and helps to clarify any misunderstandings about our work.

**References**:  
[1] MIntRec: A New Dataset for Multimodal Intent Recognition. Zhang et al. ACM MM 2022.   
[2] MIntRec2.0: A Large-scale Benchmark Dataset for Multimodal Intent Recognition and Out-of-scope Detection in Conversations. Zhang et al. ICLR 2024.  
[3] MELD: A Multimodal Multi-Party Dataset for Emotion Recognition in Conversations. Poria et al. ACL 2019.

We thank you for your valuable comments on our paper, although we acknowledge that the release of these comments after the rebuttal phase is somewhat late. It appears there may be some misunderstandings regarding the licensing terms under which our dataset was released. We will address each of your concerns point by point below.

## Reply to Data Privacy, Copyright, and Consent:

**Q1**. Use of Personal and Biometric Data

**Q1-(a)**: The benchmark relies on datasets containing videos of human interactions from sources like YouTube, Vimeo, and TV shows. These videos inherently include sensitive, personally identifiable information, such as faces and voices, which constitute biometric data. 

**A1-(a)**: We would like to emphasize that **all the datasets used in our benchmark are preserved in their original form**. Each dataset's license explicitly allows use for research purposes, as outlined in the respective publications. To clarify any potential misunderstandings, we detail the licenses for each dataset below:

MIntRec [1]: Uses clips from the TV show Superstore on YouTube, licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

MIntRec2.0 [2]: Uses clips from Superstore, The Big Bang Theory, and Friends on YouTube, also licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

MELD [3]: Uses data from Friends, licensed under the GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPL-3.0), a strong copyleft license that requires open-sourcing derivative works but imposes no usage restrictions.

IEMOCAP [4]: Contains dyadic sessions with actors performing scripted or improvised dialogues. It is distributed under a research-only, non-commercial license.

MOSI [5]: Uses video blogs from YouTube. The data has been processed into anonymized features. **The authors explicitly state that videos under Creative Commons licenses can be edited and used without the authors' consent**.

CH-SIMS v2.0 [6]: Uses Chinese TV show clips from web-sharing platforms. The authors state that these videos are under Creative Commons licenses, allowing reuse without the authors' consent.

UR-FUNNY v2.0 [7]: Uses TED Talks on YouTube, which are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 License (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), permitting non-commercial sharing and usage of subtitles and transcripts.

MUStARD [8]: Uses clips from Friends, The Golden Girls, and Sarcasmaholics Anonymous, released on YouTube under Creative Commons licenses for research use.

Anno-MI [9]: Uses videos from YouTube and Vimeo transcribed using automatic speech recognition. The authors stated that they obtained explicit consent from video owners and, where applicable, the individuals featured. The dataset is licensed under the Public Domain.

IEMOCAP-DA and MELD-DA [10]: Extend the IEMOCAP and MELD datasets with additional emotion and dialogue act annotations.

Thus, we **strictly adhere to each dataset's license**, and **we do not make any new modifications or annotations to create a new dataset**. Our work merely evaluates foundation models on these existing datasets.

**Final and most importantly**, as stated in MELD and CH-SIMS datasets [3,6], the authors clearly stated that **they consulted a legal office to verify that the usage and distribution of very short video clips fall under the fair use category**. As shown in Table 1 of our paper, the video utterances across all datasets are of very short duration, ranging from 2.4 to 9.1 seconds on average. **This further supports that the benchmark is legally valid for research use and distribution.**

**Q1-(b)**: The analysis of individuals' emotions, intentions, and behaviors raises significant privacy concerns, as the subjects may not have provided explicit consent for their data to be used in this specific research context.

**A1-(b)**: Our research follows the original intended use cases of these datasets, as established in the papers that introduced them. These datasets are widely used in the research community, backed by published papers, legal licenses, and open-source standards. For example:

- MIntRec and MIntRec2.0 [1, 2]: multimodal intention recognition
- MELD [3] and IEMOCAP [4]: multimodal emotion recognition
- MOSI [5] and CH-SIMS v2.0 [6]: multimodal sentiment analysis
- UR-FUNNY v2.0 [7]: multimodal humor detection
- MUStARD [8]: multimodal sarcasm detection
- Anno-MI [9]: motivational interviewing in counseling dialogues
- IEMOCAP-DA and MELD-DA [10]: multimodal dialogue act classification

Since we reproduce **exactly the same experimental settings** as in the original works, we believe our use aligns with the originally intended and consented research purposes.

Thanks for your suggestions. We will address your concern point by point.

**Reply to Limitations Weaknesses**: 

**Q1**. The experimental reporting lacks statistical rigor. Error bars or confidence intervals are omitted due to computational constraints, which undermines the reliability of results like the 60-70% accuracy claims.

**A1**. Thank you for highlighting this point. Zero-shot inference performance tends to produce consistent results without the need for multiple random seeds, as shown in [1, 2]. To validate the stability and reliability of model performance, we selected one LLM (Qwen2) and two MLLMs (MiniCPM-V-2.6 and Qwen2-VL) and applied supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the MIntRec, MUStARD and MOSI datasets. The average performance with standard deviations over random seeds 1–3 is shown below:

| Model | Dataset | ACC | F1 | Precision | Recall | WF1 | WP |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| MiniCPM-V-2.6 | MIntRec | 80.10 ± 0.18 | 77.75 ± 1.67 | 78.19 ± 0.48 | 78.89 ± 1.79 | 79.81 ± 0.27 | 80.51 ± 0.27 |
| MiniCPM-V-2.6 | MOSI | 86.30 ± 1.30 | 86.29 ± 1.30 | 86.45 ± 1.21 | 86.33 ± 1.28 | 86.28 ± 1.31 | 86.48 ± 1.20 |
| MiniCPM-V-2.6 | MUStARD | 67.63 ± 0.42 | 66.68 ± 0.38 | 68.70 ± 0.76 | 67.10 ± 0.30 | 66.93 ± 0.61 | 68.64 ± 0.81 |
| Qwen2 | MIntRec | 75.13 ± 0.52 | 66.44 ± 2.72 | 66.96 ± 2.88 | 67.59 ± 2.94 | 74.59 ± 1.09 | 75.53 ± 1.05 |
| Qwen2 | MOSI | 86.15 ± 0.53 | 87.68 ± 0.45 | 87.69 ± 0.47 | 87.68 ± 0.45 | 87.68 ± 0.46 | 87.69 ± 0.46 |
| Qwen2 | MUStARD | 63.04 ± 1.25 | 58.37 ± 6.15 | 67.10 ± 4.53 | 60.92 ± 3.40 | 59.52 ± 4.85 | 66.54 ± 3.80 |
| Qwen2-VL | MIntRec | 79.33 ± 0.60 | 75.96 ± 2.47 | 76.97 ± 2.59 | 76.04 ± 2.62 | 79.01 ± 0.56 | 79.45 ± 0.69 |
| Qwen2-VL | MOSI | 88.44 ± 0.17 | 88.43 ± 0.17 | 88.45 ± 0.16 | 88.44 ± 0.16 | 88.44 ± 0.17 | 88.46 ± 0.15 |
| Qwen2-VL | MUStARD | 67.39 ± 0.73 | 66.45 ± 0.58 | 67.43 ± 0.67 | 66.46 ± 0.66 | 66.94 ± 0.23 | 67.43 ± 0.69 |

From the results, we observe that on the MIntRec dataset, MiniCPM-V-2.6 and Qwen2-VL achieve highly stable performance, with error bars below 0.3% on several metrics (e.g., ACC, WF1, and WP). On the MOSI dataset, Qwen2 and Qwen2-VL show stable performance with error bars below 0.6% across all metrics. On the MUStARD dataset, MiniCPM-V-2.6 and Qwen2-VL also show stable performance with error bars below 1% across all metrics. While some metrics exhibit higher error bars, almost all remain below 5%, demonstrating the reliability of the reported results. We will include additional results with error bars and report averaged performance over multiple random seeds in the final version.

**Q2**. Dataset limitations pose reproducibility risks: some videos cannot be redistributed and require direct download from original sources, potentially hindering replication and accessibility.

**A2**. The subtitles and videos (including audio) for 10 out of the 12 datasets are all available on Huggingface and can be downloaded as a complete package, without the need to access the original sources.

For the IEMOCAP dataset, users can obtain the raw videos directly from the official website by simply filling out a short form indicating the intended use and basic information (e.g., academic research). This process usually takes only a few days. Alternatively, users may contact us for assistance in completing the form. For the MOSI dataset, we can provide preprocessed features, which are also available for download.

**Q3**. The benchmark's high difficulty, highlighted by low post-tuning accuracy, may reflect inherent data noise, but the paper only briefly discusses noise handling in Appendix F without robust mitigation strategies.

**A3**. Thank you for your valuable suggestion. There might be a slight misunderstanding in your interpretation of our paper. We argue that the low post-tuning accuracy is primarily due to **the limited capabilities of current foundation models in effectively leveraging multimodal information to understand high-level cognitive semantics, rather than being caused by inherent data noise**.

The quality of the datasets used has been ensured through strict high-quality data selection procedures during their collection. Therefore, we believe the current benchmark is sufficiently challenging to evaluate whether existing foundation models can reason effectively across semantic dimensions in multimodal scenarios.

If this benchmark can be solved with high performance, a more challenging scenario involving noisy data is discussed in Appendix F. However, that scenario is beyond the main scope of this paper.

[2] Fangyun Wei, Jinjing Zhao, Kun Yan, et al. A large-scale human-centric benchmark for referring expression comprehension in the LMM era. In Proceedings of the 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems Datasets and Benchmarks Track, 2024.

**Q1-(a)**. Why these specific aspects are essential for MLLMs' understanding of human conversational utterances?

**A1-(a)**. **We have provided the reasons in lines 126-129**: To comprehensively evaluate the complexity and diversity of human interactions, we select six representative dimensions across various linguistic and interactional levels: intent, dialogue act, emotion, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior. These dimensions collectively encapsulate the core aspects of multimodal language analysis [1, 2].

**Q1-(b)**. The paper lacks theoretical justification or prior research to support the comprehensiveness and relevance of these six dimensions. Demonstrating the motivation with references to prior studies would help better establish the importance of the proposed benchmark.

**A1-(b)**. **We have provided a comprehensive theoretical justification and references to prior research from lines 129 to 143**. For each dimension, we explain the concepts and sources with representative prior research (e.g., intent [3], emotion [4], dialogue act [5], sentiment [6], speaking style [7], communication behavior [8]).

**Q1-(c)**. Also, it remains unclear why a model must consider these six dimensions simultaneously.

**A1-(c)**. Our paper only states that these six dimensions collectively encapsulate the core aspects of multimodal language analysis (lines 128-129), rather than suggesting that they should be considered simultaneously. Moreover, in our experiments, we evaluate each dimension **individually** through various publicly available multimodal datasets for zero-shot inference and SFT, and compare the state-of-the-art methods in each field. Instruction tuning is used to validate whether a model has strong generalization capabilities across all these dimensions. This demonstrates the power of tuned MLLMs in mastering multiple cognitively challenging tasks. Finally, these six dimensions encompass a broad body of research in the entire multimodal language analysis field. Thus, our method can have a significant impact due to the lack of a benchmark for evaluating foundation models in multimodal language analysis. 

**Q2**. The contribution is limited, as the dataset is primarily constructed from existing datasets. The paper does not clearly explain the annotation process or the criteria for selecting and organizing questions from existing datasets. Therefore, the benchmark is close to a compilation of prior works.

**A2**. **Our contributions are clearly stated in Section 1 (lines 63 to 71)**. First, we do not annotate datasets for this benchmark, so there is no annotation process. We use the full version of existing, publicly available, representative datasets in multimodal language analysis across the six dimensions, and we retain the original videos and corresponding subtitles for our research. Therefore, we do not need to select or organize questions from existing datasets. Second, we notice that the focus might deviate from the core contributions of this work. As stated in lines 68-71, we have conducted extensive experiments to reveal new insights into foundation models for multimodal language analysis. These new insights can be found in Section 5.1 (lines 232-285). We also evaluate three strategies (i.e., zero-shot inference, SFT, and instruction tuning) on 12 datasets across six dimensions of five mainstream MLLMs and three mainstream LLMs, analyzing fine-grained performance and model scalability through numerous experimental results. The proposed MMLA pushes the limits of existing MLLMs, providing a solid foundation and promising new directions for further research.

**Q3**. The details regarding Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) and Instruction Tuning (IT) are not clear, such as how the training data is prepared and what the training data.

**A3**. We have introduced the methods of SFT and IT in Section 3.3. **A4**.  We appreciate your concerns regarding the scale of the dataset, particularly the time required to evaluate 61K multimodal utterances using current models. summary.value: MMLA puts today’s large language models through a tougher, more realistic test than most people realise. The authors stitch together 61 k+ utterances—roughly seventy-six hours of TV clips, movies, TED talks, social media videos and real counselling sessions—and tag every line along six human-centred axes such as intent, emotion and humour. They then pit three fashionable text-only LLMs (Llama-3, InternLM-2.5, Qwen2) against five vision-language counterparts, ranging from half-billion to 72 billion parameters, in zero-shot, task-specific fine-tune and all-in-one instruction-tune settings. The picture that emerges is nuanced: without any extra training, even the flashiest multimodal giants lag behind a well-prompted 7 B text model; yet a lightweight 7-8 B MLLM, nudged with a few LoRA updates, can suddenly match the 72 B flagships at about 68 % accuracy. A single instruction-tuned model reaches similar heights while sparing researchers the pain of juggling multiple per-task checkpoints. Still, no system breaks the 70 % barrier, underscoring just how much headroom is left in high-level multimodal reasoning. In a sentence, the paper gives the community a large, diverse benchmark, a careful head-to-head of eight model families and a sobering reminder that genuine cognitive-grade understanding of video-and-audio conversations remains an open challenge.

strengths_contributions.value:
-  MMLA spans 61 016 utterances (≈76 hours of video) drawn from nine diverse public sources—TV sitcoms, films, TED talks, social-media clips and real counselling sessions.
- Every utterance is tagged along six semantic dimensions—intent, dialogue act, emotion, sentiment, speaking style and communication behavior—providing a deep, cognitive-level multimodal analysis.
- The authors benchmark eight foundation models (three text-only LLMs and five MLLMs ranging from 0.5 B to 72 B parameters) under zero-shot prompting, LoRA-based fine-tuning and instruction tuning.
- Unlike previous datasets that focus on affective computing or low-level vision tasks, MMLA is the first large-scale suite aimed at cognitively demanding, multimodal semantics for foundation models.
- The paper is well organized—Section 3 lays out a concise taxonomy of the six annotation axes, and Table 1 efficiently summarizes label counts, clip durations and language coverage.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Six metrics are listed, but Section 4 only highlights single-seed accuracy—no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided.
- Table 1 shows all nine source corpora are English or Mandarin; there’s no representation of low-resource languages or non-Western cultural contexts.
- The paper notes 12 K utterances “reserved for testing,” but doesn’t confirm that speakers, scenes or videos don’t overlap between train and test sets.
- Results contrast LLMs and MLLMs using full inputs, yet there are no text-only, audio-only or video-only ablations—so it’s unclear whether models truly leverage non-textual cues.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value:
- Core transcripts and labels are on Hugging Face, but users still have to track down licence-restricted videos and audio separately. Please provide a simple downloader that pulls these assets automatically—or, at minimum, share precomputed CLIP/Whisper embeddings to avoid manual fetching.
- Key subsets like MOSI and IEMOCAP can’t be redistributed, forcing users to download them one by one. This breaks one-click reproducibility—consider bundling scripts or clear instructions to streamline the process.
- The dataset card omits critical metadata: no collection timeline, no consent statement for the counselling sessions, and no SHA-256 checksums. Expand it to include a detailed timeline, intended-use and consent information, plus a manifest of checksums for all files.

summary.value: This paper introduces the MMLA benchmark, a comprehensive framework for evaluating multimodal large language models in understanding high-level cognitive semantics within human conversational interactions. The benchmark spans six core dimensions—intent, emotion, dialogue act, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior—leveraging over 61,000 multimodal utterances from nine publicly available datasets. These datasets cover diverse sources, including staged scenarios and real-world settings, totaling 76 hours of video data with aligned text, audio, and video modalities. The authors evaluate eight mainstream LLMs and MLLMs using zero-shot inference, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and instruction tuning (IT).

strengths_contributions.value:
1. It addresses a critical research gap by introducing the first comprehensive benchmark (MMLA) for evaluating high-level cognitive semantics in multimodal language analysis, which has been overlooked in existing MLLM benchmarks focused on perceptual-level tasks. The benchmark's design is rigorous, covering six diverse semantic dimensions and integrating 61K samples from nine datasets, ensuring broad applicability across domains like virtual assistants and social behavior analysis. 

2.The experimental evaluation is extensive and methodical. The authors assess multiple model branches (five MLLMs and three LLMs) using three distinct methods (zero-shot, SFT, IT), providing deep insights into scalability and performance trends.

3, The work offers valuable open-source contributions. Datasets are curated under proper licenses (Appendix A), and code is publicly available on GitHub, facilitating reproducibility and community adoption. 

4.The analysis reveals novel findings, such as IT's ability to handle multiple tasks with a single model and the benchmark's role in exposing MLLM limitations, which sets a foundation for future research in human-AI interaction.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The experimental reporting lacks statistical rigor. Error bars or confidence intervals are omitted due to computational constraints, which undermines the reliability of results like the 60-70% accuracy claims. 

2. Dataset limitations pose reproducibility risks: some videos cannot be redistributed and require direct download from original sources, potentially hindering replication and accessibility. 
3. The benchmark's high difficulty, highlighted by low post-tuning accuracy, may reflect inherent data noise, but the paper only briefly discusses noise handling in Appendix F without robust mitigation strategies.

summary.value: In order to evaluate the cognitive-level semantics ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the paper introduces MMLA, a benchmark containing 61K multimodal utterances spanning six dimensions: intent, emotion, dialogue act, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior. The authors conduct a comprehensive evaluation of eight major LLMs and MLLMs under three settings: zero-shot inference, supervised fine-tuning, and instruction tuning.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper is well-structured and easy to follow, with clear and informative figures and tables.

2. The experiments are comprehensive, including closed-source models such as GPT-4o and open-sourced ones of various sizes, ranging from 0.5B to 72B parameters.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The motivation is not clear: The authors introduce six self-defined categories of questions, but it is unclear why these specific aspects are essential for MLLMs' understanding of human conversational utterances. The paper lacks theoretical justification or prior research to support the comprehensiveness and relevance of these six dimensions. Also, it remains unclear why a model must consider these six dimensions simultaneously. Demonstrating the motivation with references to prior studies would help better establish the importance of the proposed benchmark.

2. The contribution is limited, as the dataset is primarily constructed from existing datasets. The paper does not clearly explain the annotation process or the criteria for selecting and organizing questions from existing datasets. Therefore, the benchmark is close to a compilation of prior works.

3. The details regarding Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) and Instruction Tuning (IT) are not clear, such as how the training data is prepared and what the training data.

4. There are concerns regarding the scale of the dataset, specifically how long it would take to evaluate 61K questions with current models. It would be helpful to report the model evaluation time to demonstrate its practicality.

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value: Authors need to check whether it is appropriate to refer to previous datasets and build up a new one.

final_justification.value: The paper conducted comprehensive experiments on the MLLMs and LLM on 61K multimodal utterances spanning six dimensions: intent, emotion, dialogue act, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior. The complete experimental design and configurations make it an acceptable paper.

summary.value: This paper introduces MMLA, a large-scale benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to perform multimodal language analysis—a complex task that involves understanding high-level cognitive semantics such as intent, emotion, dialogue act, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior across text, audio, and video modalities.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The paper introduces MMLA, a benchmark focused on evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to understand high-level semantics in human communication. It addresses an underexplored area: cognitive-level tasks such as intent recognition, emotion classification, dialogue acts, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior — going beyond low-level tasks like object recognition or scene understanding.

- The study explores not only model performance but also scaling behavior (e.g., comparing 0.5B to 72B parameter models), and finds that smaller fine-tuned models can be competitive, which is useful for practical deployment.

- The paper compares MMLA with prior datasets like MultiBench, MELD, IEMOCAP, and others, and justifies its novelty by showing that most existing benchmarks lack either multimodal coverage or cognitive-level semantics.

- The paper is well-organized, with a logical flow from motivation to results. Figures and tables are informative and clearly labeled.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The visual design of Table 2 and Table 3 could be improved by using simpler and more consistent color schemes.

- Given that this work aims to evaluate the cognitive-level semantic understanding capabilities of large language models, I believe it would be valuable to include "misinformation detection" as an additional evaluation dimension. This is particularly relevant for real-world applications such as fact verification and content moderation. I recommend exploring this direction in future versions of the benchmark, potentially incorporating datasets such as FakeSV [1] and FVC [2].

title.value: Can Large Language Models Help Multimodal Language Analysis? MMLA: A Comprehensive Benchmark

abstract.value: Multimodal language analysis is a rapidly evolving field that leverages multiple modalities to enhance the understanding of high-level semantics underlying human conversational utterances. Despite its significance, little research has investigated the capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to comprehend cognitive-level semantics. In this paper, we introduce MMLA, a comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to address this gap. MMLA comprises over 61K multimodal utterances drawn from both staged and real-world scenarios, covering six core dimensions of multimodal semantics: intent, emotion, dialogue act, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior. We evaluate eight mainstream branches of LLMs and MLLMs using three methods: zero-shot inference, supervised fine-tuning, and instruction tuning. Extensive experiments reveal that even fine-tuned models achieve only about 60~70% accuracy, underscoring the limitations of current MLLMs in understanding complex human language. We believe that MMLA will serve as a solid foundation for exploring the potential of large language models in multimodal language analysis and provide valuable resources to advance this field. The datasets and code are open-sourced at https://github.com/thuiar/MMLA.
